item.title: What’s Missing From Trump’s Midterm Convention
item.description:
One thing is missing from President Trump’s midterm gathering for Republicans this week: any semblance of official party business that forms the backbone of traditional quadrennial conventions.

Essentially, Mr. Trump has stripped out all the perfunctory, yet necessary, parts of a typical presidential convention and kept the made-for-TV elements.

Only once before in modern political history, in 1982, has a national party held a midterm-year gathering in advance of the midterm elections. That event, held by Democrats, went so poorly that the next party chairman called such events “places for mischief” and canceled plans to do it again in 1986.

In Dallas, there will not be a roll call of states awarding delegates to a presidential nominee. There won’t even be a presidential nominee. Or voting delegates. Forget about subcommittees to determine the party’s rules and credentials.

Republicans will not be debating their party platform, though they did not really do that at the last two presidential conventions, either. By now, the party’s platform is generally whatever Mr. Trump decides it is.

Instead, the two-day gathering in Dallas is set to be a pair of six-hour — though perhaps much longer — advertisements for Mr. Trump and his political acolytes. The speakers are a parade of Trump supporters, many of whom are either in his cabinet or on the ballot this November.

Party conventions in presidential years usually take place in the summer, are scheduled to avoid the Olympic Games and are meant to be held when there are few other compelling TV options. This event comes after Labor Day and will compete for national attention against the first two nights of the N.F.L. season.

The 1982 Democratic midterm conference, as it was called then, followed similar events in 1974 and 1978 that were held in December, after the midterm elections. They were essentially kickoff events for the coming presidential elections — though in 1978, Senator Edward M. Kennedy upstaged President Jimmy Carter with a speech that foreshadowed their contentious primary campaign.

Last year Ken Martin, the Democratic National Committee chairman, floated holding a midterm convention, but the idea was quietly dropped.

Some things in Dallas will look familiar. Vice President JD Vance, who is set to speak on Thursday night, will play the role of potential future presidential contender. His speech will be inspected for both his loyalty to Mr. Trump and indications of his possible ambitions for 2028.

And you can bet that Mr. Trump will preside over a balloon drop, or maybe two of them. They were known to be among his favorite parts of the 2016 and 2024 conventions — and a spectacle that had to be skipped in 2020 when Republicans moved their convention outdoors because of the coronavirus pandemic.

item.title: Iran’s Strikes on Base in Jordan Caused Limited Damage, U.S. Officials Say
item.description:
Iran’s bombardment overnight Tuesday of a military base in Jordan used by American forces resulted in “minimal” damage to equipment and caused no deaths, two U.S. officials said on Wednesday.

But the officials warned that some service members may come forward in the coming days to report traumatic brain injuries, a common feature of such strikes.

Eighteen American service members have been killed and scores have been injured since the war began more than six months ago. The Pentagon has provided little information about U.S. casualties unless they were serious, citing operational security.

The barrage of strikes on the base were the latest volley in what is becoming a regular series of tit-for-tat strikes between Washington and Tehran, as Iran’s leaders show a willingness to escalate the conflict.

Iran targeted Jordan after the U.S. military said on Tuesday that it had destroyed five Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for attempted strikes on a U.S. Navy warship.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps called the strikes a “punitive operation” and said that they would “continue,” according to Iranian state media.

The Jordanian military said that it had intercepted 18 of the 20 missiles and that two had fallen in unpopulated areas. But the two U.S. officials acknowledged that the base in Azraq, Jordan, was hit.

The attacks occurred three days after Iran made its first known attempt at striking an American military vessel.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed responsibility for the attacks on a U.S. aircraft carrier and destroyer, saying it fired ballistic missiles at them for “harassing Iranian ships.”

Both countries appear to be stuck in a cycle that is draining U.S. air defenses and deepening Iran’s economic crisis.

As of last month, the Pentagon had used more than 1,500 Patriot interceptor missiles in the war and had fewer than 1,700 interceptors left, according to two people briefed on the stockpile levels who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military details. The United States produced about 600 interceptors in all of 2025.

At the same time, President Trump’s naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, an economically vital waterway, is making it nearly impossible for Iran to ship oil, its main source of revenue.

Mr. Trump has tried to pivot from a military campaign to one focused on choking its economy, but fighting has flared in recent days as each side jostles for control of the strait.

U.S. military officials have vowed to strike three Iranian ships for every two vessels hit by Tehran. But Iran has continued to fire on ships, throttling the world’s oil supply, to preserve one of its biggest sources of leverage.

The result has been a stalemate.

The U.S. military’s Central Command said the Iranian tankers it targeted on Tuesday were “part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the I.R.G.C. and its regional proxies,” referring to the Revolutionary Guards. It said the attacks came after Iran fired ballistic missiles at a Navy warship twice in two days.

item.title: Hunter Biden’s Crypto Offering Plummets Upon Launching
item.description:
Hunter Biden’s new novelty crypto token flopped Wednesday morning, losing more than 95 percent of its value in a matter of hours of its launch.

The son of former President Joseph R. Biden Jr. had criticized President Trump’s own such token, called a memecoin, as a “grift.” Critics immediately said the younger Mr. Biden’s was no different.

In a social media post Tuesday night on X, Mr. Biden presented his new coin partly as a mechanism to make charitable donations. He did not address whether and how he would personally benefit, but creators of memecoins can profit from transaction fees or if their own tokens rise in value.

Memecoins are akin to collectibles, with no intrinsic value. Their worth is driven purely by demand and speculation.

Mr. Biden’s coin, $LAPTOP, started trading at $37.26, jumped to $222.75 within minutes, then plummeted to $1.34 by midafternoon, according to CoinMarketCap, a website that monitors crypto prices.

The token’s name refers to his laptop, the source of controversy when it was discovered in a computer repair shop and its contents leaked before the 2020 election. Materials on the computer added fuel to concerns about his foreign business dealings; the Biden campaign rejected the accusations.

In a late-afternoon post on X, Mr. Biden blamed predatory traders and technical problems for driving up the token’s price. He said the price had stabilized to a “healthy” level.

Mr. Trump took in a whopping $636 million from sales of his $TRUMP memecoin last year, according to his latest financial disclosure. That represented more than a fourth of the minimum of $2.2 billion in revenue he reported.

But many purchasers of that coin lost out when it crashed in value, according to Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm. As of the middle of last year, 58 buyers had gained a total of about $1.1 billion in profits. Some 764,000 crypto wallets, most with small holdings, lost money, the firm’s data shows.

The president’s coin, having once peaked around $74, was selling Wednesday for $2.15, slightly more than Mr. Biden’s. Melania Trump’s token, introduced along with the president’s on the eve of Inauguration Day, was selling for 11 cents, down from a high of around $14.

Critics of memecoins claim they are often no more than “pump-and-dump” schemes, where creators and early buyers hype the coin, then cash out before the value tumbles. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission can bring civil charges if it finds fraud.

Mr. Biden denounced Mr. Trump’s coin as a scam in his media post while trying to drive up interest in his own offering, flagging an article in The Wall Street Journal about its debut.

“Why would I ever want to support a memecoin? Why something that has been so misused by grifters?” he wrote. He discouraged buying his coin as an investment, saying that “you should not expect me or anyone else to make this token more valuable for you.”

Instead, Mr. Biden, who says he is sober after a history of drug addiction, promoted it as a symbol of “resilience, redemption and recovery.”

As the coin nose-dived, social media critics let loose. “You, Trump, Melania, and the others are just ripping people off who support you,” one wrote on X. “You are truly no better.”

item.title: Military Aide Accidentally Deploys Emergency Slide on New Air Force One
item.description:
A military aide accidentally deployed an inflatable emergency slide on the new Air Force One on Wednesday, delaying President Trump’s departure to Dallas, according to a person familiar with the episode.

Mr. Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews that officials were just checking on the slide. He did not acknowledge it had been inadvertently deployed.

“They want to make sure everything works perfectly,” he said, noting that he would be delayed only about 15 minutes.

Mr. Trump eventually took off on the plane to Dallas, where he is attending the Republican midterm convention.

“As the president has said, the slide was checked out to make sure everything works perfectly,” Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, said in a statement. “Air Force One is on its way to Dallas so he can deliver his much-anticipated speech to a raucous and sold-out crowd.”

The White House declined to share any details on the incident, but the emergency escape slide in the Boeing 747-8 operates in a fashion similar to an airbag, as it is rapidly inflated in an emergency with high-pressure compressed gas cylinders.

After the slide has been deployed, it has to be carefully folded and inspected before it can be reinstalled and the inflation mechanism has to be reset and certified.

But to get a plane back in service more quickly, a replacement emergency slide device could be installed with certified technicians, according to documentation about the system published by aviation parts suppliers.

The new Air Force One, a 747-8, has an unusual evacuation slide because one of its doors is high off the ground and requires an abnormally long slide that has to be extendable, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

The deployment of the inflatable slide marked the latest challenge in Mr. Trump’s efforts to fly on the new presidential aircraft, which was donated by the Qatari government.

Once the U.S. government took ownership of the plane, it was quickly retrofitted so that the president could start flying it as soon as possible. The New York Times reported that the Qatari jet lacked defensive capabilities that the older models have.

Concerns about the new plane’s capabilities came under more scrutiny when Mr. Trump took it to the NATO summit in Turkey in July. Multiple people with knowledge of the matter said that there had been a security concern about his flying aboard the Qatari plane.

Mr. Trump declared that he would fly on one of the older presidential aircraft for his departure, instead of the Qatari jet that he had flown aboard to Turkey, for “old time’s sake.”

Although he boarded the older plane at the airport in Ankara, Turkey, it later emerged that the president had been whisked off it and onto a military jet, leaving the older Air Force One aircraft as a decoy flight.

Eric Lipton contributed reporting.

item.title: Election Officials Grapple With Uncertainty as Supreme Court Considers Mail Ballot Plan
item.description:
Election officials in Madison, Wis., mailed 18,000 ballots on Tuesday, more than a week ahead of the state’s targeted date, just to get them out the door. In Weber County, Utah, officials are considering setting up distribution centers for voters to retrieve their mail ballots and bypass the Postal Service completely.

Across the country, election officials are grappling with the confusing implications of the Trump administration’s proposed mail ballot screening plan, which would allow the Postal Service to determine which ballots can be delivered to voters.

A federal judge has halted implementation of the system, which has been challenged as unconstitutional by two dozen states. The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to intervene and allow it to go forward ahead of the midterm elections, which will determine the balance of power in Congress.

While they wait for the court’s order, local election officials are trying to sort out how they would comply with the new rules, which would require states to use federally approved envelopes with bar codes unique to each voter and upload voter data to an online Postal Service portal, which is not yet operational.

“Quite frankly, we don’t even really have a way to prepare because we don’t know when that ruling is going to come down, and then we’re going to get state guidance, and then we are crunching up closer and closer to Election Day,” said Lisa M. Deeley, the Democratic vice chair of the Philadelphia City Commissioners, which runs elections and voter registration for the city. The city is planning to start mailing ballots next week.

“It’s just chaos,” she added.

Some states, including North Carolina, Delaware and Alabama, have already mailed out their ballots, raising serious questions about how they could retroactively comply with the new system if it is put into place.

It is not clear whether or how the Postal Service would verify previously mailed ballots if the new rule goes into effect.

“We have not been provided any further information regarding their process for verifying the ballots,” said Kristin Mavromatis, the spokeswoman for the board of elections in Mecklenburg County, N.C.

On Wednesday, the chief election officials in seven G.O.P.-controlled states filed a brief to the Supreme Court, arguing that it was too close to the midterms to make any major changes to how elections are conducted.

The brief, which was signed by the Republican secretaries of state in Kentucky, North Dakota, South Dakota, Georgia, New Hampshire and Kansas, as well as the lieutenant governor of Utah, broke with the Trump administration’s effort to significantly restrict mail voting ahead of the 2026 elections. They were joined by 26 current county and local election officials and five former election officials.

In signing the brief, the secretaries of state in Kansas and South Dakota found themselves on opposite sides from those states’ attorneys general, who were part of a Republican-led state coalition arguing in support of the administration’s mail voting plans. The Missouri Association of County Clerks and Election Authorities also broke with their attorney general in signing the brief.

Their disagreement was not necessarily on the policy; rather, it was on the timing.

“Attempting to implement the rule now will almost certainly lead to mistakes, delays and confusion for both voters and election officials,” the brief states.

Many election experts say the plan could make it nearly impossible for some Americans to vote by mail because it would create impediments to the delivery of their ballots.

“It would be massively disenfranchising, and it would serve no real purpose, because the government didn’t make any showing that this rule is actually going to prevent any fraud, or even that they could put their rule in place,” said Richard L. Hasen, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, who specializes in election law.

Mr. Hasen said that the rule would especially hurt rural, disabled and elderly voters who often cannot easily get to polling locations.

Justin Roebuck, the Republican County clerk for Ottawa County, Mich., a conservative district with one-quarter of its voters casting mail ballots, said the rule appeared to do little to accomplish what the Trump administration has argued is its purpose — to increase voting security.

“So we are actually not accomplishing what the end goal was, but we are going to inconvenience millions of voters across the country — certainly, thousands in my community,” he said.

Under the Constitution, states are responsible for carrying out elections. The states that are challenging the Trump administration’s new plan say that it creates a federal role in elections because the Postal Service would reject ballot envelopes that do not comply with the new standards and send them back to local and state officials to fix.

“That comes dangerously close to playing a role in the administration of elections, which the Postal Service has always, always eschewed,” William Hensley, a former Postal Service official who worked with local election officials on best practices for ballot delivery, said.

The Postal Service has denied taking on a new election administration role, saying that states have complete control over voter registration data.

The agency did not respond to requests for comment this week. In a statement on Friday, the postmaster general, David Steiner, said, “Regardless of political party or perspective, we share a common goal: ensuring that Americans can have confidence that their election mail will be handled securely and delivered reliably should their election officials choose to use the mail for ballot delivery.”

Some of the requirements in the rule — such as those that would standardize federal ballot envelopes and create unique bar codes for voters that the Postal Service can easily read automatically — could improve the process, some elections officials and lawyers said. But, they added, it is impossible to accomplish those changes in time for the Nov. 3 elections.

“These are all good things,” said Eric Fey, the Democratic elections director in St. Louis County, Mo. “But if people haven’t been doing it, it can’t be implemented overnight.”

Missouri is one of 12 states that joined the Postal Service in defending the rule in federal court. The state has said it would be able to comply if the Supreme Court gives the Trump administration the green light, although Mr. Fey said he told the state’s top election official that some counties could not comply because they do not have federally approved envelopes or Postal Service bar codes.

In Utah, a deeply red state that votes almost exclusively by mail, some local officials are discussing abandoning mail voting entirely if the Supreme Court allows the Postal Service to restrict the practice.

With envelopes already printed and ballots coming soon, Ricky Hatch, the Republican clerk in Weber County, Utah, said that it is too late for his county to comply with the proposed federal requirements. Officials are considering setting up backup ballot distribution centers.

“We’re going to have to figure out how are we going to get these ballots into the hands of the voters,” Mr. Hatch said, adding: “It will be expensive and challenging and some voters will be disenfranchised, and it will be confusing.”

In their brief to the Supreme Court, the G.O.P. election officials noted that many of the states had already designed and printed their mail ballot envelopes.

Getting new envelopes would normally take four to eight weeks from vendors. A crush of thousands of municipalities needing new materials could stretch that timeline to 12 to 16 weeks, well beyond Election Day in November, the officials noted.

Some election officials have also expressed alarm about the Trump administration’s requirement that states upload their voter data to a Postal Service portal. The Postal Service would then only deliver ballots to those on the lists.

Elections are usually administered by individual counties, and standardizing voter registrations even within a single state is a challenge, local officials noted.

Some Texas counties have struggled with the state’s election management system that was launched last summer, said Dyana Limon-Mercado, the Democratic clerk in Travis County, one of the largest in the state.

Ms. Limon-Mercado said that certain voter registrations have been disappearing from the state system. At one point, the state system did not accept hyphenated names, she said. “I have no confidence that this state system that is also unstable and still buggy is going to connect to some federal system that we haven’t seen yet or tested yet,” she said.

Zach Montague and Nick Corasaniti contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: As Republicans Gather in Dallas, Talarico Offers a Different Show
item.description:
James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, gathered supporters on Wednesday at a South Dallas food drive to thank them for collecting groceries and to offer some counterprogramming to President Trump’s midterm convention several miles north.

In a community center, next to a towering pile of boxed, bottled and canned foods — Cheerios, veggie sticks and refried beans — Mr. Talarico railed against the “billionaire megadonors” he said would be “clinking their champagne glasses” at the Republican event.

“While we’re here serving our neighbors,” Mr. Talarico said, “they are toasting to their own corruption.”

His Republican opponent in the race, Attorney General Ken Paxton, was set to speak on Wednesday at the convention.

The food drive was one of two events that the Talarico campaign was holding in Dallas as a counterpoint to Republicans rallying behind President Trump in a downtown arena. The Texas Democratic Party was set to have their own event later on Wednesday near the convention, featuring a slate of other statewide candidates, including those running for attorney general and lieutenant governor. And several Democratic congressional candidates also planned an event on Thursday.

The Texas Democratic Party also paid for a moving billboard attacking Mr. Paxton to drive around Dallas on Wednesday, accusing him of “protecting pedos” because of his office’s handling of a child sex case. (Mr. Paxton’s campaign has said the case was resolved with the child’s interests in mind and has accused the Talarico campaign of “retraumatizing” the victim.)

Mr. Talarico also went on Fox News and offered what appeared to be a more moderate position on transgender athletes in sports than he has taken in the past.

“I oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness,” he said in the interview. “Every sport has to be safe and fair. As a former public school teacher, I care a lot about our student athletes.”

As polls have shown a close race, with Mr. Talarico leading by a narrow margin in some surveys, Mr. Paxton has also begun talking about lowering prices, modulating a hard right message that has helped him win with Republican voters. Mr. Paxton issued a news release on Tuesday reminding Texans that, as attorney general, he had secured a settlement in June with producers over high prices and would soon distribute more than five million eggs to food pantries across Texas.

Frederick Douglass Haynes III, a pastor and a Democratic congressional candidate in Dallas, introduced Mr. Talarico, and mocked the Republican convention.

“It’s a pep rally, and I’m tripping because what are you cheering?" Mr. Haynes said. “Are you cheering the fact that we’re losing when it comes to the economy, we’re losing when it comes to health care, we’re losing a war that is unconstitutional, unnecessary, and unwinnable?”

Mr. Talarico’s campaign said that the goods had been collected by volunteers and weighed over 20,000 pounds — a number designed to contrast with the $20,000 ticket price said to have been charged to some Republican attendees at the convention.

The groceries were intended for middle-class Texas families, the campaign said.

Among those in attendance was the former county judge for neighboring Tarrant County, Glen Whitley, a Republican who left office in 2022 and has grown disillusioned with his party’s rightward shift. He now supports Mr. Talarico.

“I truly believe that Ken Paxton is the most corrupt politician we have in Texas,” Mr. Whitley said in an interview. But, he added, Mr. Paxton “might have to take a second place, since Trump’s in Texas right now.”

item.title: Trump Administration Accuses Berkeley Law School of Racial Discrimination
item.description:
The University of California, Berkeley, discriminated against white and Asian applicants to its law school, the Justice Department and the Education Department said Wednesday.

The move expands the Trump administration’s effort to enforce its contested interpretation of a three-year-old Supreme Court ruling that struck down race-conscious admissions programs. It also escalates the government’s clash with the University of California system. All 10 of its campuses have come under federal scrutiny.

The Justice Department based its findings, in part, on applicant data provided by the law school, which it said showed that the school had a bias against Asian and white applicants and in favor of Black applicants.

Harmeet K. Dhillon, the Justice Department’s top civil rights official, wrote in a letter to a lawyer for Berkeley that the patterns “could not reasonably have occurred by chance and provide substantial evidence of intentional discrimination.”

Berkeley fired back soon after the Justice Department released Ms. Dhillon’s letter.

“Berkeley is committed to ensuring that every student is admitted based on their merit, and not on their race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin,” the university said in a statement, adding that it would “spare no effort to provide ample evidence showing that the university complies with all relevant laws, policies and rules governing admissions.”

The administration’s approach to college admissions stems most directly from a Supreme Court ruling in 2023, in which Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. wrote for the majority that applicants must be treated as individuals and “not on the basis of race.”

But he also said the ruling should be not “construed as prohibiting universities from considering an applicant’s discussion of how race affected his or her life, be it through discrimination, inspiration or otherwise.”

During President Trump’s second term, the Justice Department has contended that the court had forbidden any consideration of race in admissions processes. It has argued that some of the factors that colleges might use to boost students’ applications, such as being a recipient of the need-based Pell grant, were being used as proxies for race.

In the case of Berkeley, according to the Justice Department, the law school had used “race, essay prompts and other tactics to further its admissions diversity goals.” The result, the government contended, was that Black applicants were far more likely to be admitted to Berkeley’s law school than white or Asian applicants with comparable qualifications.

In a statement, Ms. Dhillon said Berkeley had shown “a complete disregard for the rule of law.”

Although the government has demonstrated some interest in undergraduate admissions procedures — it has a pending investigation, for instance, at Yale — the Justice Department’s formal accusations have so far focused on law or medical schools.

The University of California system has been a persistent target: The Justice Department has already accused the medical schools at the Davis, Los Angeles and San Diego campuses of wrongdoing in admissions.

Those accusations flow from the web of investigations that the Justice Department has pursued against U.C. campuses for almost all of Mr. Trump’s second term. The agency assigned a special group to investigate the university system and last year sought more than $1 billion to settle antisemitism claims at U.C.L.A.

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the Education Department have also been examining California campuses.

An Education Department inquiry into Berkeley provoked a campus furor last year, after university officials gave the Trump administration names of students and employees who were tied to complaints about antisemitism.

Leaders at Berkeley sought to distance themselves from the move, which a campus lawyer wrote at the time that it was in response to “directions” from system officials. But the Berkeley chancellor, Richard K. Lyons, faced enormous backlash on the campus, where many people argued that the university had capitulated to pressure from the government.

item.title: Trump’s Midterm Convention May Struggle for Ratings Against the N.F.L. Kickoff
item.description:
President Trump prides himself on his television ratings. But on Wednesday night, his speech at the Republicans’ midterm convention will confront one of the few forces in American culture that reliably draws a bigger audience than the president: the National Football League.

Mr. Trump’s remarks, scheduled for around 9 p.m. Eastern time, will coincide with the first game of the N.F.L. season, a Super Bowl rematch between the New England Patriots and the Seattle Seahawks, which is set to air on NBC. (On Thursday night, when Mr. Trump is scheduled to speak again, a San Francisco 49ers-Los Angeles Rams game will be streaming on Netflix.)

The football games are likely to siphon away millions of viewers who might otherwise watch the Republican gathering. Roughly 28 million people tuned in for last year’s N.F.L. opener.

The Republican gathering in Dallas this week, engineered by Mr. Trump as a party-boosting spectacle ahead of the midterm elections, is likely to struggle to match the mass audiences that the traditional nominating conventions achieve in presidential election years.

ABC, CBS and NBC say they have no plans to pre-empt prime time shows for Wednesday or Thursday’s festivities, as they typically do for the quadrennial party conventions. CNN and MS NOW said they would air their usual evening programs and pivot to Dallas if news warranted.

For those wanting to follow along in Dallas, countless streaming services and online outlets, including The New York Times, will carry a live feed. On cable, C-SPAN is planning full coverage, while simultaneously airing speeches by Democratic candidates on C-SPAN2.

Fox News is airing a special two-hour “Hannity” on Wednesday and Thursday beginning at 9 p.m. Several of the network’s other programs, including Bret Baier’s 6 p.m. newscast, have relocated to the American Airlines Center in Dallas for the event.

NewsNation is planning to air speeches by Mr. Trump and Vice President JD Vance. A spokesman for Newsmax said that the channel would air the most newsworthy portions — about 25 percent of the proceedings, he estimated.

item.title: A Hostile Trump Reopens Old Wounds in the U.S.-Canada Relationship
item.description:
The invasion of Canada was to be swift and overwhelming.

U.S. forces would take the port city of Halifax before seizing power plants near Niagara Falls. More American troops would storm across the border to capture Montreal, Quebec and other key cities. The secret U.S. military plan, known as War Plan Red, even authorized the use of poison gas.

The assault was never seriously considered. Drafted in 1927 and declassified decades later, it was a contingency plan for a highly unlikely war.

History took the opposite path: In the century since, the United States and Canada have been two of the friendliest and most integrated nations ever to share a border.

Until recently, that is.

President Trump has thrown the U.S.-Canada relationship into its greatest crisis since his country’s northern neighbor became self-governing in 1867. Accusing Canada of unfair trade practices, Mr. Trump has instigated a trade war that on Tuesday led Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada to retaliate with tariffs targeting roughly $20 billion in U.S. imports. Mr. Trump in turn escalated with bans on imports of some Canadian motorcycles, alcoholic beverages, dairy products and molasses.

Mr. Trump is hardly the first U.S. president to feud with Canada, especially on economic matters. Trade disputes shook relations for much of the 20th century, though they became far less common once the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement came into force.

Other heated cross-border disputes have flared on matters ranging from Alaska’s Yukon border to whether Canada would allow American nuclear weapons on its soil.

But Mr. Trump’s hostility toward Canada features a nationalist streak that goes well beyond economics. He has taunted its leaders as weaklings, denigrated its military as ineffective and even challenged its sovereignty. In particular, his talk of claiming its 3.9 million square miles of territory as a “51st state” has inflamed longtime Canadian anxieties about American domination, and even invasion.

At times he even intimates violence, as in a recent Truth Social post depicting himself and Mr. Carney in hockey gear, with Mr. Trump standing over a fallen Mr. Carney as though he has just body-checked the Canadian leader.

“I think it’s actually impossible to find a period where things were as bad,” said Robert Bothwell, a professor emeritus at the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs who specializes in U.S.-Canada relations. “There’s never been an occasion, ever, where an American president has said the annexation of Canada was his objective.”

Before Mr. Trump came along, the popular American image of Canada was one of a friendly, harmless and perhaps somewhat dull junior partner to the United States. The notion of cross-border conflict was the stuff of satire. The 1995 Hollywood comedy “Canadian Bacon” imagined an unpopular U.S. president who whips up popular resentment toward Canada to distract from his domestic struggles. Now Canadians ask whether the movie was prescient.

Canadians have always been warier of the United States, according to Christopher Sands, the director of the Center for U.S.-Canada Relations at Johns Hopkins University’s School of Advanced International Studies.

Canada was formed by several British colonies that had never broken with London, unlike their American counterparts. Seeing the growth of U.S. economic and military power as a potential threat, they joined together in the name of collective strength while remaining part of the British Empire well into the 20th century. (War Plan Red did not reflect such a threat: It imagined a U.S. attack on Canada as a defensive response to war with Britain.)

Quarrels over a common 5,525-mile border were largely settled in a 1908 agreement, one that Mr. Trump has called invalid.

But economics still roiled the relationship. After Congress approved a 1911 agreement to drop tariffs on major Canadian imports, conservatives in Canada attacked it as a threat to the country’s independence — not entirely without justification.

“I look forward to the time when the American flag will fly over every square foot of British North America up to the North Pole,” Representative Champ Clark, a Missouri Democrat who would soon become speaker, declared during a House debate on the measure.

A backlash resulted in Canada. According to Mr. Bothwell, some Americans were stopped on the street and forced to sing “God Save the King.”

Cold War politics produced more clashes. Canada fought alongside the United States in both world wars and joined the United States as a founding member of NATO. And President John F. Kennedy celebrated the relationship in a grandiloquent 1961 address to Canada’s parliament: “Those whom nature hath so joined together, let no man put asunder,” he declared.

But Mr. Kennedy lashed out at Canada’s prime minister when he resisted the placement of certain U.S. nuclear weapons on Canadian soil that were intended to deter the Soviet Union, and when he hesitated to place Canada’s military on heightened alert during the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962.

An even greater shock came in the form of Richard Nixon’s 1971 move from the gold standard and imposition of 10 percent tariffs on all imports, including Canadian ones. While many countries were affected, none were quite so dependent on the U.S. economy as Canada.

After a heated December 1971 meeting at the White House between Mr. Nixon and Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, Mr. Nixon declared the Canadian a “pompous egghead” and a “son of a bitch.” Mr. Trudeau later responded that he had “been called worse things by better people.”

Mr. Nixon abandoned the plan months later. Mr. Sands said the economic disruption it created wound up driving support for greater free trade across the border, culminating in the 1994 NAFTA agreement. (Mr. Trump has derided that Clinton-era pact as a “nightmare,” and renegotiated it during his first term under the rubric of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or U.S.M.C.A.)

The shock of Mr. Nixon’s economic gambit also boosted Canadian mistrust of U.S. economic intentions. In 1973, the Canadian political thriller “Ultimatum” depicted an American president’s demand for free access to Canada’s vast oil and gas reserves.

Canada’s prime minister resists, but the American president refuses to take no for an answer.

“As of this moment, Canada will become part of the United States of America. The government of Canada is hereby dissolved,” he declares at its conclusion.

“Ultimatum” became the year’s best-selling book in Canada.

Few expect Mr. Trump to go that far. Mr. Sands said Mr. Carney could still strike a deal to defuse the crisis. But he also warned that the dispute had unleashed forces that may take on a life of their own.

“Trump has pushed the nationalist buttons in Canada,” Mr. Sands said. “As long as Carney resists, it’s good for his politics.”

“The Canadians have really been shocked by this,” he added. To restore relations, he said, “we have to win the Canadian public back over — and that’s going to take a long time.”

item.title: How Much Does Trump Care Who Wins the Midterms?
item.description:
Stop me if you’ve heard this one before: President Trump is convening Republicans in Dallas tonight for a highly unusual, two-day convention, with less than two months to go until the midterms.

The gathering, which has come to be called Trump-a-palooza by Republicans and Democrats alike, will place the president and his policies at the center of Republicans’ midterm messaging. (Follow the reporting from my colleagues on the ground in Dallas here.)

It’s not clear whether this will help Republicans whose battleground races could determine control of Congress — and it’s not clear, either, how much Trump cares whether or not it does.

As the confab kicks off in Dallas, I asked my colleague Maggie Haberman, a White House reporter and an expert on the president, to tell us what she knows about Trump’s midterm approach. Here’s our conversation:

In a midterm year, a president often travels the country to help his party. Trump has stayed pretty close to Washington, although you’ve reported that that’s about to change. How much is he thinking about the midterms?

This is one of those questions where the answer might change depending on when you ask it. For the most part, according to all of our reporting, he is not spending a ton of his mind share on the races themselves.

He’s been spending a lot of time on his legacy projects for himself — not legislation, but the triumphal arch, the ballroom on the White House complex, his goldification of the Oval Office and other parts of the West Wing.

He’s been telling advisers, according to our reporting, that people should be doing more to defend what he sees as his many accomplishments, which is why there are now some videos circulating from his team that focus on those topics.

Is that what he wants the midterms to be — a referendum on him, and a chance to buttress his accomplishments? Does he see the midterms as another legacy project?

I think that attaches a bit too much strategery to how he’s looking at it, to quote Will Ferrell pretending to quote President George W. Bush. Trump was indifferent to the midterms in 2018, when he and his son-in-law and formal adviser at the time, Jared Kushner, believed they would benefit from having Democrats as a foil, but also as a group they could make deals with.

The president now basically views himself as untouchable. He has the Supreme Court’s presidential immunity ruling that protects sitting presidents from criminal liability for official acts, and he has said he will pardon anyone, in his words, who has come within a certain radius of the Oval Office.

Remember, he has told people that he is “proud” that Republicans don’t do as well when he’s not on the ballot. THAT is the legacy project for him.

This brings us to his midterm convention. A lot of Republicans might like to be out campaigning, but instead, they’re in Dallas. Who is this for?

There’s no question this was conceived of as something enjoyable for Trump, and multiple advisers to the president have conceded that privately. A number of Republicans facing tough campaigns are staying away.

It’s a big party for Trump at a moment when a lot of Republicans are anxious about what his policies, including on trade and the war with Iran, mean for the economy and for their chances of getting elected. Can they expect help from the president? And in what form?

A great question, and one that was not answered by the $10 million laid out from his super PAC, MAGA Inc., in the last few days to support Ken Paxton, the party’s controversial Senate candidate in Texas. That amount of money is not going to help other groups figure out how to budget their own spending.

However, Teddy Schleifer, Shane Goldmacher and I reported earlier today that a new mystery PAC, is tied to Trump’s political orbit and appears to be a vehicle through which his super PAC is now spending much more of the hundreds of millions of dollars that it has on hand. This week, the new group reserved at least $49 million in advertising to aid Republicans in key Senate races in states like Ohio, Michigan and New Hampshire.

It’s the biggest midterm-related outlay so far from a pot of funds that Trump has referred to, while speaking with reporters, as “my money.”

Then there’s his promised travel, although how much of it he will do remains an open question. Someone like Senator Susan Collins of Maine, who has her own political identity, almost certainly would rather not spend a ton of time with the president. But since Republicans mostly see this as a turnout election, and not a persuasion election, the majority of Republican candidates will make the most of it.

There is another way Trump could shape the midterms. His administration is also working to restrict mail voting. How focused is Trump on this, and how do he and his advisers think it will affect the elections in November?

There’s the significant X-factor of what he is attempting to do with restricting mail-in voting based on what he keeps claiming, but never proving, is widespread voter fraud significant enough to affect the elections he’s made such claims about. He’s extremely focused on that, and his rallying cry of “rigged” elections, which he has used both when he’s won (2016 general election) and when he’s lost (2020 and the 2016 Iowa caucuses).

Not everyone in his group of advisers favors approaching it this way, but regardless, it is potentially going to inject confusion into the process.

This interview was edited and condensed.

There is something missing from Trump’s midterm gathering, Reid Epstein writes: any semblance of the official party business that forms the backbone of the traditional conventions you might be used to seeing in a presidential election year.

There will be no roll call. No voting delegates. No wonky subcommittees. Instead, the two-day gathering is basically a pair of six-hour advertisements for Trump and for Republicans.

If you are tuning in, here are five things Reid thinks you should look out for.

ABOUT LAST NIGHT …

New Hampshire’s Senate race is expected to be tight, as I wrote over the weekend. Jeanne Shaheen, the Democrat who now holds the seat, is retiring, and Republicans think they have a shot at flipping her seat. Last night, voters picked the candidates who will run to replace her.

Democrats chose Chris Pappas, a moderate congressman. Republicans went with John E. Sununu, a former senator whom Shaheen unseated nearly two decades ago.

There was also a compelling primary in the First Congressional District. Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of the retiring senator, claimed the Democratic nomination. She’ll face Anthony DiLorenzo, a Trump-backed businessman.

In a year when so many primaries have featured insurgent progressive victories and shocking upsets, the results were surprising in their own way. Read more of my takeaways here.

LIL’ RHODY

Voters in Rhode Island are casting ballots today. (Yes, it’s a Wednesday. Primary season never rests!) There’s a Senate race, and a few statewide offices. But the main event is the Democratic primary for governor, where the incumbent could be in trouble.

Gov. Dan McKee, 75, is seeking a second term. He’s running against a challenger who almost beat him in 2022, Helena Foulkes, a health care executive. And this time around, he has some baggage: His abrupt closing of a bridge in 2023. McKee shut the bridge down for safety reasons, but Rhode Islanders are still fuming over the disruption, my colleague Jenna Russell reported. A recent poll from Emerson College showed Foulkes leading by 15 points.

Polls close tonight at 8 p.m. Eastern. You can follow the results here.

one last thing

It’s not just MAGA Inc. that’s giving out money. Trump himself doled out $45,000 in Christmas gifts to a select group of White House staff members — including to Natalie Harp, the ever-present aide whom some Democrats are trying to turn into a midterm punchline.

Taylor Robinson contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Trump’s Census Overhaul Would Exclude Some Immigrants and Remove Questions on Race
item.description:
The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed to no longer count immigrants without green cards in the 2030 census or ask about race and ethnicity, part of an overhaul that would redefine who counts as a U.S. resident in the eyes of the federal government.

The sweeping measures would upend a process that helps determine the allotment of congressional seats, billions of dollars in federal funding and policies to address systemic disparities.

The proposed regulation, published online on Wednesday, would not count noncitizens without green cards in the 2030 census, a significant departure from the process stipulated by the Constitution to occur every 10 years. Historically, the census has asked Americans about their race and ethnicity and counted all U.S. residents regardless of their immigration status.

The overhaul also would bar the U.S. census from asking Americans about their sexual orientation.

While the proposal is likely to face legal challenges, the changes would not only remove undocumented immigrants from the official population count used to determine congressional seats, but also immigrants who are in the United States legally and have yet to secure green cards or citizenship. As a result, areas with more immigrants, which tend to vote Democratic, could lose representation and federal funding.

The proposed overhaul, as well as removing questions about race, ethnicity and sexual orientation from the census, could have major implications for collecting the federal data used to inform anti-discrimination policies and civil rights protections.

“If we don’t have the data in order to see that there’s problems, then we’re sticking our heads in the sand,” said Kimball W. Brace, the president of Election Data Services, an organization working with Democratic and Republican local governments on census and election issues. “We won’t see it. We won’t get a feel for what’s happened.”

An overhaul of the census count would face significant hurdles. The 14th Amendment calls for “counting the whole number of persons in each state,” rather than just citizens. And the rule would affect a census count after the 2028 presidential election, so a new administration could try to reverse the changes. Under the U.S. Constitution, Congress is tasked with carrying out the census; however, it has delegated decisions on the census to the Commerce Department.

But some researchers said Mr. Trump’s decision to try to resurrect his first-term effort to reshape the census could create a chilling effect and reduce participation.

As part of the proposal released on Wednesday, the administration said it was considering including a question in the census about the immigration status of participants, something civil rights groups have warned would deter immigrants with and without legal status from filling out the form out of fear of government retaliation.

“The Trump administration is trying to omit pieces of the population that they don’t feel are real Americans,” said William H. Frey, a demographer at the Brookings Institution. “And in many ways, pulling back some of the trends and important policies that came into effect since the civil rights movement of the 1960s.”

The White House referred questions to the Commerce Department, which did not respond to requests for comment.

In the proposed rule posted on Wednesday, signed by Mr. Trump’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, the administration said it was reassessing how it collects race and ethnicity data after “substantial doubts about the meaning, significance, and impact of attempting to categorize persons by race and ethnicity” surfaced in the national conversation.

The proposal also cited Mr. Trump’s executive order that purged the federal government of efforts centered on diversity, equity and inclusion.

The release of the regulation came after Mr. Trump last year ordered the Commerce Department to exclude undocumented immigrants from the census. “People who are in our Country illegally WILL NOT BE COUNTED IN THE CENSUS,” Mr. Trump wrote in a post on social media in the summer of 2025.

The proposal on Wednesday, however, went further by trying to exclude those immigrants with legal status who lack a green card.

The administration argued in the proposed rule that undocumented immigrants are not “true inhabitants” of the United States because of “their lack of a sufficient tie and allegiance” to the country. And while some immigrants without green cards have legal status, the administration said in the proposal that such status is “less durable and indefinite in length.”

Mr. Trump began a similar effort in his first term when he sought to add a citizenship question to the 2020 census. The effort ultimately failed.

A federal court rejected the attempt, and the Supreme Court declined to intervene. Career officials in the Census Bureau, which is part of the Commerce Department, also stood up to the administration’s attempts to exert pressure on their work.

Attorney General Letitia James of New York said on social media on Wednesday that her office was exploring legal options to challenge Mr. Trump’s proposed changes.

“The Constitution is clear,” Ms. James said. “Every person living in the United States, regardless of immigration status, must be counted in the census.”

item.title: Fetterman Has a Surprise Cameo at Trump’s Convention
item.description:
Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, the self-proclaimed champion of working-class voters who has become alienated from his own party and fed up with his job, on Wednesday appeared in a short video on the opening night of President Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas.

“Yes, I’m a Democrat. Why am I here talking to you today?” Mr. Fetterman said in a video filmed in front of a steel mill in Pennsylvania. He introduced himself as a “common-sense Democrat” who said he is “always going to reject the extremes in socialism.”

Mr. Fetterman introduced Senator David McCormick, Republican of Pennsylvania, and said that they would work together “and work with President Trump and defend the steel way of life.”

The appearance of a Democrat at a convention boosting the G.O.P., at a time when his party is claiming that they have made life harder and more expensive for Americans, was a boon for Republicans just weeks before crucial midterm elections in which they are battling to defend their slim congressional majorities.

And it undercut Democrats’ message as they work to focus the final crucial weeks of the midterm campaign on the president, whose approval ratings are sagging, and his unpopular policies. Instead, Mr. Fetterman’s brief comments underscored Republicans’ main argument in the campaign — that Democrats are extremists and socialists who cannot be trusted to govern.

It came amid recent speculation that Mr. Fetterman could switch parties, a move he has said he would “never” make but has appeared more likely as his breaks with his own party have become more frequent and bitter.

His decision to take part in Mr. Trump’s convention appeared designed for maximum shock value and served as a boost for Republicans’ otherwise lackluster gathering, which many of their most vulnerable incumbents and candidates have opted to skip as they work to gain some distance from an unpopular president.

At the height of Mr. Fetterman’s popularity with Democrats, he briefly harbored aspirations to run for president in 2028, according to former aides. Instead, frustrated with his own party and his standing within it, and aware of the attention he garners for criticizing it, he has sought allies on the other side of the political aisle.

In recent months, Mr. Fetterman has amped up his flirtations with Republicans, while still vowing that he would never actually switch parties. In July, he set up an unusual joint fund-raising committee with Mr. McCormick, with whom he has established a close, personal bond. And he has said that if his party officially turned against Israel, as some of its most progressive voices are urging, it would be the “red line” that would force him to leave.

But he has also been adamant that despite his disagreements with Democrats and his antipathy to party gatherings and caucus meetings, he had less in common with Republicans. In an interview in July, he told The New York Times he would “never” leave the party.

About 69 percent of likely Democratic voters in Pennsylvania view Mr. Fetterman negatively, according to a poll conducted last month by The New York Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University. Most Republicans in his state, however, now hold a positive view of Mr. Fetterman, who has become a fixture on conservative news outlets bashing the policies of his own party.

The progressive Working Families Party announced last year it would recruit and support a primary opponent to challenge him in 2028.

As Mr. Fetterman has evolved into a lawmaker who barely resembles the man he presented to voters on the campaign trail in 2022 — a champion of the underdog who highlighted his ties to Senator Bernie Sanders, the democratic socialist from Vermont — several former staff members have grown incensed and vocal in saying he is abdicating his responsibilities.

A group of his disillusioned former staff members last week threatened to begin revealing private communications from Mr. Fetterman in which he expressed disdain for the day-to-day duties of being a senator. The former staff members, who made their announcement with an anonymous account on X, said they would begin releasing the material on Monday, when the Senate returned from a weekslong break.

Mr. Fetterman was elected in 2022, after he had a life-threatening stroke in the middle of the most competitive Senate race in the country.

Shortly after being sworn in, he checked himself in to Walter Reed National Military Medical Center to be treated for depression for six weeks, and appeared to make a remarkable recovery as he began speaking out about the importance of getting help when needed. But then in 2024, he began retreating from the job, rarely attending committee meetings, casting votes or holding town halls.

He has since expressed remorse for speaking openly about his mental health and claimed that the criticism he gets for missing votes and committee hearings is because of it.

“My doctor warned years ago: After it’s public that you are getting help for depression, people will weaponize that,” Mr. Fetterman told The New York Times in an interview last year. “Simple things are turned. That’s exactly what happened.”

item.title: Trump Takes No Position on Allies’ Sanctions Against Israeli Settlements
item.description:
President Trump declined to say on Wednesday whether the United States opposed new European and Canadian sanctions against Israeli settlements, the latest in a notably muted U.S. response about penalties against America’s most important ally in the Middle East.

Speaking to reporters as he was about to depart Washington for Texas, Mr. Trump said that he was aware of the wide-ranging economic restrictions announced by Britain, Canada and France targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank over settler violence against Palestinians.

Asked whether the U.S. opposed them or remained neutral, Mr. Trump dodged the question.

“I’ll be speaking to Israel,” he said. “I’ll be speaking to them, and I’ll find out what they, what’s their thinking. I understand exactly what’s going on. But I want to find out why all of a sudden does that happen.”

Three officials with knowledge of the situation said that Mr. Trump, during a call with Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain, was briefed on the sanctions before they were announced, and that he did not push back on them. The people spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a private call.

Taken together, Mr. Trump’s response on Wednesday and his reaction during the call with Mr. Burnham speak to the president’s growing frustration with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel as the war in Iran grinds on.

The White House did not respond to questions about where the United States stood on the sanctions, whether Mr. Trump’s response signaled tensions with Israel, or its position on settler violence. Instead, a White House official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic relations, said Mr. Trump has a strong relationship with Mr. Netanyahu and commended the country’s military.

The United States and Israel jointly launched the conflict in Iran earlier this year.

Britain, Canada and France on Tuesday announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, a remarkable rebuke to Israel from once-staunch allies. The pact was led by Britain, which accused Israel of committing “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank.

The measure risked a rift with the United States, which supports Israel militarily and diplomatically. But thus far, U.S. officials who are usually quick to defend Israel have been restrained in their sparse remarks on the matter.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who notably has criticized nations who issued Gaza-related sanctions against Israeli officials, said that the United States was given a heads up about the decision, but suggested that it was theirs to make.

He told reporters on Tuesday that the United States “obviously” would not join the other nations, but stopped short of criticizing them.

“We heard their argument as to why, but look, we share the goal of stability,” he said. “We don’t want to see some uptick in violence or an uptick in conflict or tensions in the West Bank at a very tenuous time. In the region, there’s always tenuous times.”

Mike Huckabee, the U.S. ambassador to Israel, was the only U.S. official to denounce the sanctions, just days after he had a rare meeting with Palestinian Americans in the West Bank, where he denounced Israeli extremists’ attacks on Palestinians and called them “terrorists”

In an interview with the BBC, he called the British trading bans “discrimination against the Jewish people” and “irrational.”

A White House official said Mr. Huckabee’s comments were not coordinated with the White House or State Department.

William F. Wechsler, the senior director for Middle East programs at the Atlantic Council, said the potency of settler violence in the West Bank was probably driving the Americans’ ambiguity.

“There are few policies that have the potential to bring together a wide coalition in the United States, across both parties, than what is seen to be terrorism in the West Bank,” Mr. Wechsler said.

While Mr. Trump has rarely addressed settler violence, and in fact lifted sanctions placed on extremist Israeli settlers by President Joseph R. Biden Jr. upon his return to office, he has said that he would not allow the annexation of the West Bank.

The administration has also reiterated the need for stability in the region in order to implement Mr. Trump’s peace plan for Gaza, which he has described as the linchpin for peace in the wider Middle East.

Lucy Kurtzer-Ellenbogen, a senior fellow with the Middle East Institute, said the administration might see the ongoing settler violence as an impediment to Mr. Trump’s ambitions.

“They’re seeing more and more of the interconnectedness of those two fronts, and can’t let one deteriorate without the precipitous deterioration of the other,” Ms. Kurtzer-Ellenbogen said.

“If we look in the context of what this administration has said at the highest level before and what they’re not saying now,” she added, “it does credibly paint a picture of an administration that may be willing to let allies do some work here that it’s not fully opposed to. It would not be a stretch for the Israeli government to be reading less support than they may want in the silence.”

Adam Rasgon contributed reporting from Tel Aviv.

item.title: A Flyover for 9/11 in Denver, With a United Jet and F-16s, Is Called Off
item.description:
Earlier this week, officials in Denver advised residents that if they saw a commercial jetliner flying above downtown, accompanied by fighter jets, not to worry: It was just a tribute for people who died in the Sept. 11 attacks.

As the 25th anniversary of the day two Boeing planes were catastrophically flown into New York City skyscrapers drew closer, the organizers of this tribute finally had second thoughts. On Wednesday, United Airlines officials canceled the planned flyover, which was to have featured a Boeing passenger jet escorted by a squadron of F-16 aircraft. They pointed to “concerns in the community.”

On Tuesday, the Denver Office of Emergency Management posted an alert about the upcoming event to the public to prevent panic and calls to emergency lines with worries about a hijacked plane. The planes for this tribute were set to take off at 8:15 a.m. local time in Denver.

At 8:15 a.m. Eastern time on Sept. 11, 2001, United Flight 175 took off from Boston en route to Los Angeles, according to the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. It was hijacked by terrorists and flown into the South Tower of the World Trade Center in Lower Manhattan at 9:03 a.m., the second of the two planes that would take down the towers, killing over 2,700 people.

The flyover tribute would have had the planes in Denver visible around 9:03 a.m. local time.

Across the country on Sept. 11, fighter jets, including F-16s, were scrambled, according to the National Guard, and some had orders to shoot down jets that did not follow their directions.

The community response was swift. Some responders on social media called the flyover “insane,” “disgusting” and “insensitive.”

In a statement, United Airlines said it now planned to commemorate the 25th anniversary of 9/11 with events at United’s Flight Training Center in Denver, including the unveiling of a monument made from steel recovered from the World Trade Center “to honor the United Airlines crew members aboard Flight 175 and Flight 93.”

United Flight 93 took off from Newark, N.J., that Tuesday 25 years ago and was plunged into a field in Shanksville, Pa., after passengers attacked the hijackers. Seven crew members and 33 passengers died on that plane, and nine crew members and 51 passengers were killed aboard Flight 175.

item.title: Helena Foulkes Defeats Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee in Democratic Primary
item.description:
Helena Foulkes, a former CVS executive, won the Democratic nomination for governor of Rhode Island, defeating Gov. Dan McKee, The Associated Press said on Wednesday night.

Mr. McKee is the first sitting governor to lose a primary since 2018 and the first in Rhode Island in more than 30 years.

The race between Ms. Foulkes and Mr. McKee, a former lieutenant governor and mayor of Cumberland, R.I., who was seeking a second term, was combative from the start. Ms. Foulkes sought to portray Mr. McKee as an insider prone to protecting his cronies; Mr. McKee criticized Ms. Foulkes’s leadership at CVS during the opioid addiction crisis, suggesting that she could have done more to combat it.

Ms. Foulkes, 62, established an early lead in the race, tapping into lingering frustration over the state’s abrupt closure in 2023 of the Washington Bridge, a critical link between Rhode Island and Massachusetts, and the resulting chaos for commuters. She also benefited from a national wave of anti-incumbent sentiment and from a sense among voters that Mr. McKee was an accidental governor.

Mr. McKee took over the job when his predecessor, Gina Raimondo, left in 2021 to be the commerce secretary in the Biden administration. He won a full term a year later, but barely survived a primary challenge from Ms. Foulkes.

Since then, Mr. McKee, 75, has spent much of his time dealing with the bridge debacle and defending his management of the crisis, which arose when engineers discovered critical structural failures. During the campaign, he tried to paint himself as a proactive leader who had put public safety ahead of his own popularity by stepping up to address a longstanding infrastructure problem that he said others had “kicked down the road.”

But many voters saw it differently. They complained about what they saw as needless communication delays and were unhappy with Mr. McKee’s decision to keep the state’s transportation chief on the job for more than two years instead of firing him immediately after the bridge closure.

“I’ve talked to so many voters in this state who have said to me, ‘If that were my job, I would have been fired right away,’” Ms. Foulkes said during a debate with Mr. McKee.

Ms. Foulkes also promised, if elected, to hire an outsider “who knows no one” to lead the state Transportation Department, instead of having “insiders” running it. Mr. McKee bristled at her critique, calling it an insult to his team.

Adam Myers, a political scientist at Providence College, said that Mr. McKee had not been a particularly popular governor even before he shut down the bridge. Then, Mr. Myers said, “the bridge saga overshadowed all other aspects of his governorship.”

In the meantime, after nearly succeeding in her first attempt to unseat Mr. McKee, Ms. Foulkes had four years to hone her strategy and raise money.

“She started readying for a rematch with him soon afterward, so she came to this race well-prepared and well-funded,” Mr. Myers said in an email. “She has burnished an image of managerial competence, which is what Rhode Island voters seem to yearn for in their state government right now.”

The state leans heavily Democratic, but President Trump won more votes statewide in the 2024 election than he had four years earlier.

Construction on the new Washington Bridge is ongoing, and is scheduled to be complete by 2028.

item.title: Ocasio-Cortez Is Selective About Her Midterm Picks. She Went Far for This One.
item.description:
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, who has carefully picked which progressive Democrats to support in this year’s midterm elections, quietly made her way to Central Florida on Wednesday to lend her star power to Angie Nixon’s underdog Senate candidacy.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez encouraged more than 50 campaign volunteers and organizers gathered at a park in Kissimmee, south of Orlando, to devote their time and energy to spreading the word about Ms. Nixon’s campaign — weeks before a single ballot is mailed out.

“They don’t see us coming,” she told them. “My favorite way to move is, we don’t go to the flashy places. This isn’t about fighting for Miami.”

“We run up the numbers here,” she added, “and then we will rack them up everywhere else, too.”

When Florida was still a pre-eminent battleground state not long ago, much of its Democratic energy originated in South Florida. But as that region has grown more Republican, the heart of the state’s progressive movement has moved to Orlando and its fast-growing suburbs.

Ms. Nixon, who is running against Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, does not typically hold traditional rallies. Instead, she makes brief appearances intended to sign up volunteers, get them to download a canvassing app and then push them to get right to work calling voters or knocking on doors.

The strategy lifted Ms. Nixon in the Democratic primary last month, when she shocked the party establishment and won by 12 percentage points on a campaign built mainly around field work and social media, despite being vastly out-raised.

That strategy will be harder to pull off in a general election, when candidates have to reach a broader swath of voters, including independents and Republicans, in a big, diverse state that is expensive to campaign in.

Ms. Nixon has challenged Ms. Moody to debate her. On Wednesday, a local Jacksonville television station said Ms. Moody had declined its debate invitation, citing an answer that Ms. Moody gave in a television interview on Tuesday in which she called Ms. Nixon “truly anti-American.” In response, Ms. Nixon called Ms. Moody in a statement “runaway Ashley.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, a potential contender in the next presidential election, endorsed Ms. Nixon last week, but she did not promote her Florida trip. The only news reporter in attendance at the event on Wednesday was a photographer for The New York Times. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez told the volunteers that she had earlier stopped by a local bakery. Kissimmee is heavily Puerto Rican, and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez is of Puerto Rican descent.

“It’s good to be backed by people who are not bought and paid for,” Ms. Nixon said at the event.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was introduced by another big supporter of Ms. Nixon’s: Representative Maxwell Alejandro Frost, the first Gen Z member of Congress. Mr. Frost, along with other local officials, has assembled a progressive coalition that campaigns year-round in Central Florida for progressive candidates and issues.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez promised to defend Ms. Nixon against racist attacks such as the one Laura Loomer, the far-right influencer allied with President Trump, made against her and other Black politicians. (Ms. Loomer described Ms. Nixon and others on social media as “ghetto Black communist,” with a crude epithet tacked on at the end.) That way, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said, Ms. Nixon — who joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June — might remain focused on campaigning as an unapologetic progressive.

“What we seek to prove,” she said, is that Democrats do not have to run from “some very unimaginative, unambitious place in order to win a statewide election.”

“The way that we do it is by being uncompromising in how visionary and ambitious we want to be for people,” she added. “And to say with our whole chest, ‘We will guarantee health care to every American.’ We can do it without taking big money, we can do without having to compromise our values. We can fight for it all.”

Zack Wittman contributed reporting.

item.title: Democrats Say Fetterman’s G.O.P. Convention Video Had ‘the Persuasiveness of a North Korean Newscast’
item.description:
By now, Pennsylvania Democrats are used to Senator John Fetterman making nice with Republicans. But his 65-second video appearance on Wednesday night at President Trump’s midterm convention ignited a new round of anger and condemnation from Democrats toward a senator they widely view as a political apostate.

Former Representative Conor Lamb, whom Mr. Fetterman beat in the party’s 2022 primary race for Senate, said the video had “all the persuasiveness of a North Korean newscast.”

Mr. Lamb is one of several Pennsylvania Democrats who say they are weighing running for Senate in 2028, when Mr. Fetterman will be up for re-election. Mr. Lamb said party officials in the state had “already assumed Fetterman is a non-factor” in a future race.

Mr. Fetterman has become increasingly estranged from his fellow Democrats since Mr. Trump returned to office last year. While he has remained a reliable vote for Democratic causes in the Senate, Mr. Fetterman has served as a leading cheerleader for Mr. Trump’s war with Iran and for Israel during the conflict in Gaza.

In Washington, Mr. Fetterman long ago stopped participating in routine meetings with Senate Democrats, whom he infuriated by establishing a joint fund-raising committee with Senator David McCormick, the Pennsylvania Republican he introduced in his video on Wednesday.

Polling released last month from The New York Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University found that Mr. Fetterman’s popularity with the state’s Democrats had cratered and that he was now far more popular with Republicans.

Mr. Fetterman has said he will “never” switch parties. He did not immediately respond to messages on Wednesday.

Representative Chris Deluzio, a Democrat who, like Mr. Fetterman and Mr. Lamb, hails from western Pennsylvania, said the senator was “making it harder” for state Democrats to win races in November by giving the impression that there is bipartisan support for Mr. Trump.

“If the Republicans want him, they can have him,” said Mr. Deluzio, who said he was also considering a Senate run in 2028. “This guy is not going to be a senator after 2028.”

And Lt. Gov. Austin Davis, who said he had been encouraged to think about running for Senate, accused Mr. Fetterman of misunderstanding the political moment.

“There is a time and place for bipartisanship, but this isn’t it,” he said. “If you willingly participate in this, you’re part of the problem.”
